Name: parametric_interference
Title: Crowded Neighbors: How Parametric Knowledge Interference Predicts When LLMs Retrieve the Wrong Fact
Short Hypothesis: Facts stored in an LLM's weights interfere with one another during retrieval when they share representational structure (a common subject, relation, or answer-token region). We hypothesize that (1) the number and representational proximity of 'competitor' facts sharing a subject/relation predicts, at the single-example level, whether retrieval of the correct fact will succeed or fail; (2) many known-but-wrong errors are actually intrusions of a nearby competitor rather than random noise or missing knowledge; and (3) a lightweight, competitor-aware retrieval intervention that suppresses the interfering direction can restore the correct answer.
Related Work: Qiao et al. (2026, DKI) study AB-AC interference but only for facts updated *in context* (multi-update prompts), not facts stored in weights; their conflict is between context versions, ours is between co-stored parametric facts. Mohan & Sen (2026) and MEMIT work model interference at *edit time* (which batches of edits collide), not at *retrieval time* for un-edited knowledge. Peng et al. (2026) discuss logic/fact superposition but focus on unlearning to distill a logic core, not on fact-fact retrieval collisions. Geva et al. (2023) and Fierro et al. (2024) dissect single-fact recall circuits without considering competing co-stored facts. Yu et al. (2023) study fact-vs-context competition, not fact-vs-fact parametric competition. Our contribution is the first study to (a) define and measure parametric fact-fact interference from internal representations, (b) show it predicts and *causes* known-but-wrong errors as competitor intrusions, and (c) provide a competitor-suppression intervention validated with false-positive controls.
Abstract: Language models store millions of facts in shared weights, forcing many facts into overlapping representational neighborhoods. We ask whether this crowding causes retrieval failures: when a model 'knows' fact A but the question also evokes a nearby competitor fact B, does B intrude on the answer? We call this parametric knowledge interference, and distinguish it sharply from in-context knowledge conflicts and from edit-time collisions. We build a benchmark that, for a target fact (subject-relation-answer), identifies competitor facts that share the subject (same subject, different relation), share the relation (different subject, same relation), or share the answer-token region (semantically nearby answers). We quantify each target's 'interference load' from internal representations: the number of competitors and the cosine proximity of their answer-position retrieval directions. We test three claims. First, interference load predicts per-example recall success (AUROC on held-out relations), beyond a difficulty baseline. Second, among known-but-wrong errors—where the correct answer is decodable in mid-layers but not produced—we measure what fraction are competitor intrusions (the produced token matches a specific high-proximity competitor) versus random errors, and validate causally via activation patching that suppressing the competitor's direction restores the correct token. Third, we introduce a competitor-aware retrieval nudge: at inference we subtract the estimated interfering direction at the answer position and measure recovery rate, false-positive rate on facts with no competitor (must not hallucinate), and side effects on unrelated queries. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 across scales, characterizing whether interference grows or shrinks with scale.
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: From CounterFact/T-REx, select ~4k target facts (subject-relation-answer). For each, build competitor sets: (i) SAME-SUBJECT competitors (other relations of the same subject with different answers), (ii) SAME-RELATION competitors (other subjects, same relation), (iii) SAME-ANSWER-REGION competitors (facts whose answer token is semantically nearby in unembedding space). Verify baseline recall so we know which targets the model can answer at all. 2) INTERFERENCE-LOAD MEASUREMENT: For each target and its competitors, extract the answer-position retrieval direction (mid/late-layer residual difference-of-means that best decodes each answer token). Define InterferenceLoad = (#competitors weighted by cosine proximity of their retrieval directions to the target's). Also compute a control 'difficulty' feature (answer token frequency, target logit margin in isolation). 3) PREDICTIVE TEST: Train a classifier to predict per-example recall success from InterferenceLoad; report AUROC on held-out relations and the incremental AUROC over the difficulty-only baseline (to show interference adds signal). 4) INTRUSION ANALYSIS: Among known-but-wrong errors (correct answer decodable via mid-layer probe/logit lens but not produced), classify each produced token as (a) a specific competitor fact's answer, (b) a plausible paraphrase, or (c) unrelated. Report the competitor-intrusion fraction and whether intrusions preferentially match high-proximity competitors. 5) CAUSAL VALIDATION: For intrusion errors, use activation patching / directional ablation to suppress the intruding competitor's answer-position direction and measure whether the correct token is restored; compare to suppressing a random direction. 6) COMPETITOR-AWARE NUDGE: At inference, subtract the estimated interfering competitor direction (scaled by alpha) from the answer-position residual. Measure RECOVERY RATE on interference-driven errors, FALSE-POSITIVE rate on no-competitor facts (should not degrade or hallucinate), and SIDE EFFECTS on a control set of unrelated correctly-answered queries. Baselines: no intervention, generic random-direction subtraction, CoT prompting. 7) SCALING & GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (410M/1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); report whether InterferenceLoad's predictive power and intrusion fraction shrink with scale (do bigger models 'de-crowd' knowledge?). METRICS: predictive AUROC and incremental AUROC over difficulty baseline, competitor-intrusion fraction, causal restoration rate, nudge recovery/false-positive/side-effect deltas, scaling trends.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Mid-layer decodability may overstate 'knows'; we require causal patching corroboration and treat it as necessary-not-sufficient. 2) InterferenceLoad may correlate with generic difficulty; we explicitly control by reporting incremental AUROC over a difficulty-only baseline. 3) Competitor-set construction is heuristic and may miss true competitors or include spurious ones; we validate causally (only directions that causally alter output count as real competitors). 4) The nudge risks suppressing the correct answer if the competitor direction overlaps it; we measure side effects and false positives as success criteria. 5) Some known-but-wrong errors will be genuine noise, not intrusions—quantifying this split is itself the informative result. 6) Effects may be architecture-specific (GQA vs MHA); we characterize across families/scales rather than assume universality. 7) Answer-region proximity in unembedding space may not equal semantic competition; we cross-check with human-judged or embedding-based semantic relatedness.
